rows.reason: Lines 8-9 'without even waiting to put on his coat' shows the sudden rush; locking and eating are correctly named as the other senses of bolt.
'of happy birds' is on line 18 after 'carol'; birds singing a song gives the key and the Christmas-song sense is set aside.

'So the row is his noise and fuss' - 'They' and 'his' have no referent in the script (rabbits/Mole never named), and it never points to lines 23-24 (the Mole bowling over the rabbit and chaffing the others), the only evidence that the noise is the Mole's, which the key asserts.

'It comes before 'round face'. So a grave face is serious and calm.' Position before a noun does not show the meaning; the key is announced, not reached, and nothing rules out 'Very sad and upset' (the 'same twinkle in its eye' on line 49 is the evidence that does).
Line 59 'unfastened a rope' then line 63 'made fast' shows tying up; 'smartly' correctly carries the speed, disposing of the 'went quickly' distractor.
Line 65 'seated in the stern of a real boat' places the word as a boat part, sets aside the stern-look sense; true and readable.

'Read line 21 to the full stop' misleads: the first full stop on line 21 is after 'cousin', before 'party' appears; the sentence ends on line 23. Also 'five people are named' is false - only Mr Bingley is named; the others are described.

'One countenance is 'pleasant', the other 'forbidding'. So it means a face' - pleasant and forbidding fit manners just as well, so the step does not separate the key from the manners distractor (line 24 joins countenance and manners with 'and'); the key is announced, not shown.
In Darcy's speech (lines 53-56) the sisters are set aside as dance partners because they are engaged, so their dances are promised; marriage sense named and set aside.
'pleasant girls' is on line 58; Bingley's ease contrasted with Darcy finding no available partner (lines 55-56) shows 'hard to please'; shy and tidy set aside.
'tolerable' on line 66 is followed by 'but not handsome enough to tempt me' (66-67), giving 'only just good enough'; tolerant correctly named as the putting-up-with word.
Line 71 'great spirit' read on to line 72 'a lively, playful disposition' gives lively and cheerful; ghost sense set aside.

'So attitude here is something her body showed' never points to 'the tense rigidity' (line 6), the words that show it is how she held herself, and 'something her body showed' does not separate the key from 'How shy and awkward she looked'. 'The word 'expectation' beside it' is loose: it is four words before 'attitude'.

'The words after it tell you what the room is for' presupposes the key (scope = room) before any evidence, and 'the room' reads as the ladies' waiting room on line 14, the room she refused to go into, which misleads.
Lines 6-9: a level bridge near flood height, yet people 'did not mind it' because of the rails, so the rails must be strong; true and teaches the inference.

'What a horse is given on arriving is food and rest.' This states the key as a general fact rather than showing it from line 14; nothing in the passage evidences 'rest', and the 'long wait with nothing to eat' distractor (the master's business took a long time, lines 14-15) is not addressed.
Lines 36-38: the dead stop and still not going forward after the cut show 'stir' is about moving; quotations and line numbers correct.
Lines 1-2 tie the commotion to the whole house whenever Uncle Podger undertook a job, giving the fuss and noise he makes; true of the passage.
Lines 38-39: he takes the rule, re-measures, and gets 'half thirty-one and three-eighths inches', so it is a measuring tool; true and shows the method.
Line 21 'perished into something like a dried leaf' shows dried and crumbled; dying sense implicitly set aside; true.
Lines 43-44: she lifts the top layer out and then reaches the navy jumper underneath, giving a level of things lying on others.

'This word names how the family felt' stops at a feeling, which the distractor 'the excitement of finding a forgotten room' also is; it never shows the feeling was worry and hurry on arriving that night, nor that the room had not yet been found then.
Line 52 'Pie for breakfast!' then 'how perfectly ripping!' shows delight in the pie; the table distractor is set aside.

Child-facing form: 'find the words growing out of.' quotes the passage without quotation marks, so the sentence reads as broken and ends on a preposition; same for 'joined by and'. Content is correct (line 29, the elder and the window-shape joined by 'and'); requote and resubmit.
Lines 31-32: carrying the can round 'spoiled the effect'; asking what it spoils leads to a mood, not a result, which sets aside the dominant sense.
Lines 43-44: something ails his foot and he 'halted to the stile' and sat, so he is moving and the word is about how he moved; sets aside 'stopped'.

Child-facing form: 'find the words or at least.' quotes the passage without quotation marks and reads as a broken sentence. Also 'Line 46 shows her going up to him again' - 'drew near' is on line 45; only 'him again' is on line 46.

'So the word is about dwelling, not hatching.' 'Dwelling' (on something) is harder than the word being taught, and a child knows it as a home (it means that in other passages); the script never reaches the key's 'lingering over'. 'Its own sweet voice.' is also a verbless fragment.
Line 12 has her on the steps to receive them; line 15 'as they alighted' makes it the arrivals' action, not hers; sets aside the curtsey and came-down-the-steps distractors.

'The load is the word' does not say which word and is hard to parse; 'bought off' is an idiom a 9-11-year-old may not know; and 'Line 5 says they are ... allowed to carry a load away' - 'load of booty' is on line 6.

Child-facing form: 'find the two words joined by as well as' quotes the passage without quotation marks and is hard to parse. Also the last step ('So relish is about how much she enjoyed the taste') is announced. Ruling out speed alone does not show enjoyment.
Line 15 'abominable old rogue', and lines 15-16 show Silver using 'the very same words of flattery' on another lad, so he cannot be trusted; Jim is named in the preamble.
Lines 52-53: he would have leaped out 'if I had found the strength' but 'my limbs and heart alike misgave me', so they would not do what he wanted; true and shows the method.
